title: The Myth of the Mad Crowd
description: Le Bon's irrational crowd, and the riot and disaster evidence that overturned it

concepts.title: Le Bon and the Crowd Mind
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1895 the French writer Gustave Le Bon published The Crowd: A Study of the Popular Mind, translated into English the next year. Its claim was blunt. When people gather around a shared focus they become what Le Bon called a psychological crowd, a "single being" obeying "the law of the mental unity of crowds". Its members lose themselves: "by the mere fact that he forms part of an organised crowd, a man descends several rungs in the ladder of civilisation."

Le Bon named three causes:

  • Anonymity: because a crowd is anonymous, the sense of responsibility that normally restrains you disappears.
  • Contagion: "In a crowd every sentiment and act is contagious", so feelings spread like an infection.
  • Suggestibility: the crowd member falls into a state Le Bon compared to hypnosis, ready to turn any suggested idea straight into action.

The book carried a political message. "The age we are about to enter will in truth be the era of crowds," Le Bon predicted, and he was sure that crowds are only powerful for destruction. Crowd theory of this kind grew out of decades of political disturbance, industrial conflict and rising patriotic fervour, and it gave anxious elites a scientific-sounding way to dismiss mass politics as madness.

Even early critics kept much of the picture. The psychologist Floyd Allport argued in 1924 that there is no group mind: "the individual in the crowd behaves just as he would behave alone, only more so." On this convergence view, a violent crowd is simply violent people who have gathered in one place. Both stories still endure in the popular imagination: the "mad mob", in which ordinary people lose their reason, and the "bad mob", in which criminals find each other.1 The rest of this lesson tests them against what crowds actually do.

concepts.title: Crowds Have Limits: St Pauls and Social Identity
concepts.contentHtml:
The first serious challenge came from sociology. Ralph Turner and Lewis Killian's emergent norm theory (1957) argued that crowds only look unanimous. Their members are diverse and often ambivalent. In an unclear situation a norm emerges, shaped by striking events and "keynoting" gestures or remarks, and that norm silences dissenters and creates an illusion of unanimity. The decisive evidence, though, came from studying real riots closely.

On 2 April 1980 police raided the Black and White Café in the St Pauls district of Bristol, and rioting followed. The social psychologist Stephen Reicher reconstructed the event from participants' accounts and found that the violence had clear limits. Attacks fell on the police above all, and on financial institutions and symbols of luxury. The police were attacked only inside St Pauls and were left alone once they had left.1 When someone broke a bus window, onlookers condemned it as the work of "idiots". People were acting on a shared social identity as members of the St Pauls community, and that identity defined who counted as a legitimate target.

If you have taken the Social Psychology topic, you have met Henri Tajfel and John Turner's social identity theory. Reicher carried it into the crowd. You do not lose your identity in a crowd; you shift from a personal identity to a social one, and the group's norms then guide what you do. His later Elaborated Social Identity Model (ESIM) treats crowd events as encounters between groups. When police use force that protesters see as illegitimate, a mixed crowd can unite around a shared anti-police identity, so policing itself can turn a peaceful crowd into a hostile one.

The model has practical uses. At the Euro 2004 football championship in Portugal, Clifford Stott and colleagues watched England fans, notorious for violence, defuse trouble by policing themselves in match cities where officers intervened only in targeted ways. They traced the contrast with two riots involving England fans in the Algarve to the different contexts that different policing created.

concepts.title: Do Crowds Panic?
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask people what happens when disaster strikes a packed venue and most will say mass panic: a stampede in which everyone tramples everyone else. Disaster research keeps finding the opposite.

In late 1979 people died in a crush outside a concert by The Who at Cincinnati's Riverfront Coliseum, and media accounts described a stampede of selfish fans. The sociologist Norris Johnson analysed transcripts of interviews with concertgoers and police on duty. He concluded in 1987 that people did not stampede over others: they tried to help, and most pushing was an effort to escape the crush, not to get in.

John Drury, Chris Cocking and Stephen Reicher then brought the social identity approach to emergencies. In a 2009 study they interviewed 21 survivors of 11 emergencies, including the Hillsborough crush and the 1983 Harrods bomb. Twelve described a feeling of unity in the crowd, and those twelve also reported more helping, even of strangers, and more orderliness, such as queuing to escape.1 In accounts from over 90 survivors and 56 witnesses of the July 2005 London bombings, selfish behaviour was rare and mutual help was common. Their explanation is that shared danger creates a sense of common fate, a shift from "me" to "us", and that shared identity makes strangers look after each other. The authors were candid about the limits: survivors willing to talk may differ from those who were not, and memories of events decades old are unreliable.

The myth survives among the people who plan for emergencies. In a 2013 survey by Drury, David Novelli and Clifford Stott of 115 police personnel, 46 civilian emergency planners and 120 football stewards, the police endorsed several parts of the mass panic myth, such as the idea that fear and rumour spread like a contagion.2 Plans built on that myth treat the public as a problem to be managed, when the evidence shows crowds in emergencies usually displaying collective resilience: helping, sharing and organising themselves.

title: Grievance and the Free-Rider Puzzle
description: Why suffering alone rarely produces protest: relative deprivation, who riots, and Olson's paradox

concepts.title: Relative Deprivation
concepts.contentHtml:
Why do people rebel? The obvious answer is that they suffer. Yet the poorest and most oppressed groups are often quiet, and revolts are typically launched by groups whose conditions are rising, not falling.1 The concept sociologists reached for to explain this is relative deprivation: discontent depends less on how badly off you are than on how badly off you feel compared with what you expected, or with the people you compare yourself to.

The idea grew from a puzzling survey result. In The American Soldier (1949), Samuel Stouffer and his colleagues found that, with rank, education and length of service held constant, the branches of the US Army that offered the fewest promotions were the ones whose men rated their chances most favourably. The Air Force private, in a service with rapid promotion, felt more deprived than the private in the Military Police, where promotions were rare.2 Each soldier measured himself against the people around him.

Students of revolution had noticed something similar. Alexis de Tocqueville observed that revolutions came when governments were relaxing oppression rather than tightening it, because "evils which are patiently endured when they seem inevitable become intolerable when once the idea of escape from them is suggested." In 1962 James Davies proposed the J-curve: revolution is most likely when a long period of economic and social development is followed by a short, sharp reversal, so that expectations keep climbing while reality drops away.

Ted Robert Gurr's Why Men Rebel (1970) built relative deprivation into a general theory of political violence. In later work he defined it broadly, as the gap between what people feel entitled to and what they actually get, so that even fairly privileged groups can be moved to rebel by a sense of disadvantage. Notice what this does to the idea of grievance: it becomes subjective, a matter of comparison and expectation rather than of absolute need.

concepts.title: Who Riots? The Kerner Commission
concepts.contentHtml:
Grievance theories make a testable prediction: the most deprived people should be the ones who rebel. The United States supplied a test in 1967. Of 164 disorders reported in American cities in the first nine months of that year, the worst came in July, first in Newark and then in Detroit. President Lyndon Johnson appointed a National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders, usually called the Kerner Commission, which reported in 1968.

Many people at the time held what the commission called the "riffraff" theory: riots were the work of habitual criminals and an uneducated, Southern-born underclass. The commission found otherwise. The typical rioter was not a hoodlum, a habitual criminal or riffraff, nor a recent migrant.1 He was a teenager or young adult and a lifelong resident of the city where he rioted. He was a high-school dropout, yet somewhat better educated than his neighbours who did not riot, and almost always underemployed or in a menial job. He was proud of his race, informed about politics and deeply distrustful of the political system. In a Detroit survey of two riot areas, about 11 percent of residents admitted taking part, 20 to 25 percent called themselves bystanders, and over 16 percent said they had been "counter-rioters" who urged others to "cool it".

The rioters looked less like the most deprived and more like people with blocked chances, which fits relative deprivation. But the same data expose the theory's weak point. Most residents shared the grievances and did not riot, and in most places grievances are widespread while protest is rare. Grievance looks necessary but not sufficient. Some economists and political scientists, including Paul Collier, Anke Hoeffler, David Laitin and James Fearon, have gone further and disputed that grievance is the main driver of rebellion at all, arguing that it is driven less by grievance than by greed.2 Sociologists drew a different lesson: to explain when people act, you have to explain how they organise.

concepts.title: Olson's Free-Rider Paradox
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1965 the economist Mancur Olson turned the question around. In The Logic of Collective Action he asked not why people rebel but why anyone joins a large group effort at all. If you studied public goods in the Public Economics topic, you know the trap. A movement's gains, such as cleaner air, a new law or the fall of a dictator, go to everyone who shares the cause, whether or not they took part. Your own contribution barely changes the outcome, while protest costs you time, money and sometimes your safety. The rational choice is to free-ride: let others pay and share the benefits anyway.

So shared interests do not automatically produce collective action, and the larger the group, the worse the problem, because each member's share of the gain shrinks and nobody notices one absentee. Olson's argument was not that collective action would fail, but that organisers need some way of giving people incentives to pay their share. His answer was selective incentives: benefits or penalties that reach only those who take part. In his by-product theory, an organisation sells something members want and uses the surplus to lobby. His example was the Illinois Farm Bureau, which lobbied for farm subsidies while selling farmers low-price car insurance.

Sociologists accepted the puzzle but not all of the answer. People also join for the friendship and standing that come with taking part, and for the satisfaction of acting on their values, rewards that a narrow cost-benefit model leaves out. Mark Granovetter's threshold models (1978), covered in the Social Networks topic, showed that whether you act can depend on how many others already have, so the same crowd can tip into action or stay still. Above all, Olson moved attention from complaint to capacity. The question became how aggrieved people get organised, and that is where the next lesson begins.

title: Resources and Organisation
description: Resource mobilisation, the organised story behind Montgomery, and whether organisation tames protest

concepts.title: Resource Mobilisation
concepts.contentHtml:
When Doug McAdam went looking for a course on social movements as a student activist in the late 1960s, his university's political science catalogue listed none. He finally found movements discussed in a course on Abnormal Psychology. That was the mainstream view: movement participation reflected aberrant personalities and irrational crowd behaviour, and in a reasonably responsive democracy sensible people used the proper channels.

A new generation of scholars, many with ties to the civil rights, antiwar and women's movements, rejected that view in the 1970s. The most influential alternative was resource mobilisation theory, set out by John McCarthy and Mayer Zald in The Trend of Social Movements in America (1973) and their 1977 article "Resource Mobilization and Social Movements: A Partial Theory". Earlier studies had treated movements as spontaneous or even hysterical reactions to frustration. Resource mobilisation stressed rationality, and the importance of funding, leadership and organisation.1

McCarthy and Zald borrowed the language of economics:

  • A social movement organisation (SMO) is a formal group pursuing a movement's goals.
  • A social movement industry is all the SMOs working towards the same broad goals, competing for supporters, money and attention.
  • The social movement sector is all those industries in a society taken together.

On this view discontent is rarely in short supply; what varies is the supply of resources. Contemporary movements need money for advertising, printing, postage, lobbying and staff. In times of economic prosperity, such as the 1960s, the entire social movement sector expands because people have more discretionary resources to give. The theory explained why protest waves can come in good times rather than bad, and by the early 1980s, in Sidney Tarrow's words, it had become "a dominant background paradigm" for sociologists studying social movements.

concepts.title: Montgomery Was Organised
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is the version many people learn: on 1 December 1955 a tired seamstress named Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, and a spontaneous boycott followed. Almost every part of that story is misleading, and the real version shows why organisation matters.

Parks was a seasoned activist. In 1943 she had joined the local chapter of the NAACP and been elected its secretary, and the summer before her arrest she attended a workshop on desegregation at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee.1 "I was not tired physically, or no more tired than I usually was at the end of a working day," she later wrote. "No, the only tired I was, was tired of giving in." Nor was she the first: nine months earlier the 15-year-old Claudette Colvin had been arrested for the same defiance, without mobilising the city.

The groundwork was laid by the Women's Political Council, a group of Black professionals founded in 1946, which had pressed the mayor about the buses in 1954. When Parks was arrested, its president, Jo Ann Robinson, prepared leaflets at Alabama State College and organised their distribution. Black ministers backed a one-day boycott on 5 December, and that day 90 percent of Montgomery's Black citizens stayed off the buses.2 The new Montgomery Improvement Association, with Martin Luther King Jr as president, then ran a carpool of about 300 cars, following advice from T. J. Jemison, who had organised one during a 1953 bus boycott in Baton Rouge. The boycott lasted 13 months and ended after the Supreme Court struck down bus segregation.

In The Origins of the Civil Rights Movement: Black Communities Organizing for Change (1984), the sociologist Aldon Morris generalised the lesson. The movement's power came from Black communities organising themselves, above all through churches, which served as indigenous organisations which supplied meeting places, money, leaders and ready-made networks.

concepts.title: Does Organisation Tame Protest?
concepts.contentHtml:
Organisation has a cost, and sociologists have argued about it for a century. Robert Michels' 1911 study of the German Social Democratic Party produced the iron law of oligarchy: organised movements develop a cautious, self-protecting leadership. Leaders responsible for a large organisation on which people depend are reluctant to risk its existence, so professionalised staff tend to lose their militancy. One classic account links this caution to the failure of German socialist trade union leaders to resist Hitler in the spring of 1933.

In Poor People's Movements (1977), Frances Fox Piven and Richard Cloward turned this into a direct attack on resource mobilisation. Their four case studies were the unemployed workers' movement early in the Great Depression, the industrial strikes that built the CIO later in the 1930s, the Southern civil rights movement, and the National Welfare Rights Organization of the 1960s and 1970s. Their conclusion: poor people achieve little through the routines of electoral and interest-group politics, so their power lies in disruption, the breakdowns that happen when people defy the rules that normally govern daily life. Formal organisations did not produce these outbreaks, they argued, and often blunted them.1 In the 1930s, strikes and sit-downs spread "despite existing unions rather than because of them", and in the civil rights movement concessions were forced by mass civil disobedience.

The book offended activists as well as theorists, and the argument is not settled. Defenders of organisation point to Montgomery, where planning, leaflets and a carpool sustained a 13-month boycott, and to William Gamson's evidence (lesson 7) that bureaucratic, centralised groups won more often. Piven and Cloward reply that organisers typically spend the rare moment of mass defiance building organisations instead of escalating. Mark and Paul Engler, reviewing the debate in 2014, argue that explosive short-term mobilisation and long-term organising are both needed. You will meet the same tension in digital movements, which can mobilise vast crowds with almost no organisation at all.

title: Opportunities and Repertoires
description: Political process theory, the history of protest forms, and how the 1960 sit-ins spread

concepts.title: Political Opportunity
concepts.contentHtml:
Resources explain capacity, but movements also need an opening. In 1973 the political scientist Peter Eisinger compared protest across American cities and introduced the idea of a structure of political opportunities. Protest was most common in cities whose political systems mixed open and closed features. The usual reading is that fully closed systems make protest hopeless, while fully open ones let grievances flow through normal channels.

Doug McAdam's Political Process and the Development of Black Insurgency (1982) built this into political process theory. Injustice in the South was old, so anger alone cannot explain why the civil rights movement rose when it did. McAdam pointed to a series of linked changes that opened the political system: the decline of cotton markets, Black migration to the North, the expansion of the Black vote, and the electoral shift to the Democratic Party.1 He added a mental ingredient, cognitive liberation: people must come to blame the system rather than themselves, and to believe it can be changed. Openings help produce that belief.

The logic travels. As the Soviet Union took steps between 1985 and 1989 to open discourse and politics, protest increased dramatically. Researchers also count the absence of repression and the presence of allies inside government, such as courts, sympathetic agencies or opposition parties, as opportunities. In nondemocracies, revolutionary movements often begin as reform movements during a period of liberalisation and radicalise only once the regime closes the reform process down. This echoes Tocqueville: the most dangerous moment comes when a regime loosens its grip.

The approach has critics. Jeff Goodwin and James Jasper, in essays collected in Rethinking Social Movements (2003), charged political process theory with a structural bias, and their book's subtitle, Structure, Meaning, and Emotion, names what they thought was missing. An opportunity only matters if people perceive it and decide to act. That challenge fed directly into the research on frames and identities in the next lesson.

concepts.title: Repertoires of Contention
concepts.contentHtml:
How do you protest? You might march, sign a petition, join a boycott, strike or occupy a square. The historical sociologist Charles Tilly, whose idea of contentious politics appears in the Revolutions and Movements topic, showed that this menu is neither natural nor unlimited. Every place and time has a limited repertoire of contention, a set of forms that people know how to perform and that authorities recognise. In Tilly's words, these "standard forms are learned, limited in scope, slowly changing, and peculiarly adapted to their settings".

Tracing contention in Britain and America between 1750 and 1830, Tilly found the repertoire transformed. The older one was parochial, particular and bifurcated: embedded in the routines, relations and communal identities of daily life, and different from place to place. The newer one was cosmopolitan, modular and autonomous: forms such as the demonstration and the petition campaign that anyone could use, anywhere, for any cause, detached from local routines. Tilly saw this newer repertoire as having developed with the social movement itself.1

That makes the social movement a historical invention rather than a timeless feature of politics; his book Social Movements, 1768–2004 traces it across more than two centuries. Its characteristic performances are displays of what Tilly called WUNC: worthiness, unity, numbers and commitment. A sober march in Sunday clothes signals worthiness; matching banners signal unity; the size of the crowd signals numbers; willingness to be arrested signals commitment.

Tilly also tied repertoires to regimes. Social movements concentrate in democracies, especially high-capacity ones, while violent political performances are most characteristic of low-capacity nondemocratic regimes. Repertoires change slowly, by innovation at their edges. The lunch-counter sit-in, the subject of the next concept, is a good example of a new form that, once invented, could be copied almost anywhere.

concepts.title: How Protest Spreads: The 1960 Sit-ins
concepts.contentHtml:
On 1 February 1960 four Black students from North Carolina A&T College, Joseph McNeil, Ezell Blair, Franklin McCain and David Richmond, bought a few items at the Woolworth store in Greensboro, North Carolina, then sat down at the lunch counter reserved for white customers. Asked to leave, they politely refused. By the end of the month sit-ins had taken place at more than 30 locations in 7 states, and by the end of April over 50,000 students had participated.1

Waves like this, often called cycles of protest, are where the study of diffusion begins. How did the tactic travel? Kenneth Andrews and Michael Biggs (2006) traced the spread of sit-ins across Southern cities, comparing the cities where sit-ins occurred with the majority where they did not. They tested three channels:

  • Movement organisations played an important role, but what mattered was a cadre of activists rather than mass membership.
  • Social networks between cities showed little evidence of carrying the protest.
  • News media were crucial, conveying information about protests elsewhere.

Sit-ins were also most likely where there were many college students and where Black adults had more resources and autonomy: news only became action where local capacity existed. Training mattered too. In Nashville, James Lawson led workshops on Gandhian nonviolence, and students who attended them, including John Lewis and Diane Nash, would later become leaders of the Southern movement.

The sit-ins show a repertoire changing in real time. The form was modular in Tilly's sense: anyone could copy it at any segregated counter, and it fed directly into the creation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). The finding that media rather than personal ties carried the wave between cities is worth remembering for lesson 7, where digital media carry protest faster still.

title: Frames, Identities and Recruitment
description: How movements make meaning, build a sense of 'we', and recruit through personal ties

concepts.title: Framing: Making Grievances Mean Something
concepts.contentHtml:
By the mid-1980s structural theories could explain when movements had the capacity to act, but not why people became convinced they should. The answer came from framing. You may know the idea from the Bias and Framing topic, where Erving Goffman's Frame Analysis (1974) and Robert Entman's definition explain how journalists shape stories. David Snow and colleagues applied it to movements in a 1986 paper on frame alignment: movements do not simply voice grievances that already exist; they work to link their interpretation of events to the interpretations of potential recruits.

Snow and Robert Benford (1988) identified three core framing tasks, which together turn a grievance into a reason to act:1

  • Diagnostic framing defines a problem or injustice and assigns blame.
  • Prognostic framing develops a plan to solve it.
  • Motivational framing supplies the appeal to join: why you, and why now.

Framing is how McAdam's cognitive liberation happens. Social arrangements must come to be seen, in Piven and Cloward's phrase, as "unjust and mutable", which usually means a shift from blaming yourself to blaming the system. A frame succeeds when it resonates with what people already believe and experience.

Some frames become master frames that many movements borrow. The "civil rights" frame of the African American freedom struggle was adopted in variant forms by the women's, gay and bisexual, Mexican American, Asian American and disability movements, and by conservative movements such as the pro-life and home-schooling movements. Latecomers to a cycle of protest, Snow and Benford argued in 1992, must align their frames with its master frame. Frames also cross borders: during the Gulf War, peace movements in many countries used the same slogan, "No Blood for Oil", yet mobilised differently in each.

concepts.title: Collective Identity: Building a 'We'
concepts.contentHtml:
In the 1970s and 1980s several European scholars, among them Alberto Melucci, argued that the movements that followed the 1960s (the women's, gay rights, environmental and peace movements) differed in kind from the old labour movement. They called them new social movements. As the state reached into private life, Melucci argued, domains such as sexual relations, biological identity, birth and death, illness and ageing, and our relationship to nature had "entered the realm of 'public' conflict".1 The new movements set out to reclaim them, and they cared as much about identity and recognition as about redistribution.

From this work came the concept of collective identity: the qualities and characteristics that members attribute to their own group. Crucially, it is built in action. Participants develop a sense of "we-ness" by taking part; in Melucci's phrase, they "communicate, influence each other, negotiate and make decisions", continually re-creating agreement about goals and strategies. Collective identity is a product of a movement as much as a precondition for one.

Social psychology tells the same story from inside the crowd. In his study of the "Battle of Westminster", a violent confrontation between students and police at a demonstration in November 1988, Stephen Reicher traced how students were drawn into the conflict, how it spread and how involvement changed them. Social categories, he concluded, are constructed and reconstructed in the dynamics of intergroup interaction. Emotion matters too. James Jasper described the moral shock: an event so at odds with your sense of how the world should be that it can launch a movement.

Critics of the "new social movement" label point out that older movements were also about identity and culture, and that newer ones still pursue laws and policies. What lasted was less the claim of novelty than the insight that identity is something movements make.

concepts.title: Who Joins? Networks and Freedom Summer
concepts.contentHtml:
Why do some sympathisers act while others who share their beliefs stay home? In 1980 David Snow, Louis Zurcher and Sheldon Ekland-Olson argued that the answer lies in social networks: people are recruited through existing ties far more than by ideas alone. The sharpest test came from Doug McAdam's study of Freedom Summer.

In the summer of 1964 about 1,000 volunteers, most of them white Northern college students, went to Mississippi to register Black voters and teach in Freedom Schools.1 Letters had warned them that arrest was likely. One week after the first group arrived for training, three civil rights workers, James Chaney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman, disappeared; their murdered bodies were found weeks later. McAdam obtained the original applications and compared 720 people who went with 241 accepted applicants who did not. Participants were distinguished from withdrawals primarily by more organisational affiliations, more prior civil rights activity, and stronger and more extensive ties to other participants.

Three ideas follow. High-risk activism usually requires deep integration into a movement's culture, often built through earlier rounds of low-risk activism. Biographical availability matters: married people with children and full-time jobs have less discretionary time, and spouses and employers may object.2 And movements grow fastest through bloc recruitment, signing up whole groups and organisations at once, as Montgomery's churches did.

The effects also ran the other way. Surveying 212 volunteers and 118 no-shows in 1983–84, McAdam (1989) found that the volunteers had been more politically active throughout the 1960s and still were, and that they were much less likely to be married and had significantly lower incomes. One summer redirected their lives. In the language of the Social Networks topic, this is complex contagion: costly, risky behaviour spreads through repeated reinforcement from several close contacts, not through one passing tie.

title: Why Civil Resistance Works
description: Chenoweth and Stephan's findings on nonviolence, the 3.5% rule, its caveats and its critics

concepts.title: Nonviolence Versus Violence
concepts.contentHtml:
Erica Chenoweth began as a sceptic. When she started a fellowship at Harvard's Belfer Center in 2006, she believed in the strategic logic of armed resistance and suspected that only violent force had achieved major political change. A workshop pushed her to prove it. With Maria Stephan she spent two years collecting data on every violent and nonviolent campaign from 1900 to 2006 that sought to overthrow a government or win territorial liberation:1 323 maximalist campaigns, analysed on nearly 160 variables. The results, published as Why Civil Resistance Works (2011), turned her expectations upside down.

An updated count in 2020 covered 565 campaigns that had both begun and ended between 1900 and 2019. About 51 percent of the nonviolent campaigns succeeded outright, against about 26 percent of the violent ones.2 Here "success" means the government fell, or independence was won, because of the campaign and within a year of its peak.

Why should unarmed movements beat armed ones? Chenoweth and Stephan's answer centres on participation. Joining a strike or a march asks far less of you than joining an armed group, so nonviolent movements can expand in ways armed groups cannot, and they tend to be larger, more cross-cutting and more representative. Size and breadth create openings for defections that pull a regime's pillars of support out from under it:

  • security forces refuse orders to shoot at demonstrators, as in Serbia in 2000;
  • business and economic elites start voicing support for the movement;
  • unions and professional associations stop cooperating, as in Sudan's revolution of 2019.

Armed campaigns, by contrast, give a regime a justification for violent counterattack and make defections less likely. The effects also outlast the campaign: countries with nonviolent campaigns were about ten times likelier to become democracies within five years than countries with violent ones, whether or not the campaigns succeeded.

concepts.title: The 3.5% Rule and Its Caveats
concepts.contentHtml:
In a 2013 TEDx talk Chenoweth added an observation that has since become a slogan, the 3.5% rule: no government in her data had withstood a challenge in which 3.5 percent of its population was mobilised against it during a peak event. That sounds small, but it is a great many people. Chenoweth put it at about 11.5 million people in the United States in 2019. The ONS estimated the UK population at 69.3 million in mid-2024, so in the UK it would mean about 2.4 million people active at once.1

Chenoweth has been careful about what the figure means. In a 2020 paper she set out the caveats:

  • It is a descriptive statistic about past movements, not a prescription. Reaching 3.5 percent without building a broader public constituency guarantees nothing.
  • It counts peak participation, not popularity. Large turnouts are usually the tip of an iceberg of wider sympathy.
  • It covers only maximalist campaigns, which aim to remove a government or win independence, so it cannot simply be extended to reform movements.
  • It has exceptions. Bahrain's uprising of 2011–2014 appears to have failed decisively despite over 6 percent participation at its peak; the regime relied on outside forces, including Saudi troops.2 Updated data also include a failed 1962 armed revolt in Brunei by a group equal to about 4 percent of the population.
  • Most mass nonviolent movements that have succeeded did so without ever reaching 3.5 percent.

The rule, in her words, is "a tendency, rather than a law". Momentum, organisation, strategic leadership and sustainability are probably as important as sheer numbers, and they are often what make large numbers possible in the first place. That is a point about causation worth holding on to: a huge crowd may be a sign of a movement's strength as much as its source.

concepts.title: Decline and Doubt
concepts.contentHtml:
The 2010s should have been nonviolent resistance's golden decade. They saw more of it than any decade since 1900, with no fewer than 96 nonviolent maximalist campaigns launched, far above the previous record of 60 in 2000–2009. Yet success collapsed. From the 1960s until about 2010, revolutionary nonviolent campaigns succeeded more than 40 percent of the time, reaching 65 percent in the 1990s. Since 2010, fewer than 34 percent have succeeded, though violent campaigns did even worse, at 8 percent.1

Chenoweth offered several explanations in 2020:

  • Smaller movements: average peak participation fell from 2.7 percent of the population in the 1990s to 1.3 percent after 2010.
  • Over-reliance on demonstrations, at the expense of more disruptive techniques such as general strikes and mass civil disobedience.
  • Digital organising, which assembles crowds quickly but builds less durable capacity (lesson 7).
  • Violent fringes, which movements increasingly tolerate and which give regimes a pretext for repression.
  • Learning regimes, which have developed savvy repression, such as infiltrating movements to divide them and provoke violence.

The core finding is also under challenge. In a 2023 replication of Why Civil Resistance Works, Christoph Dworschak found its main results highly sensitive to variable selection, to cases that may have been missed (a "streetlight effect"), and to omitted variable bias.2 A 2026 preprint by John Holbein and Charles Crabtree, not yet peer reviewed, goes further: it reports misreported results and fragile models, and concludes that the cross-national data give no clear basis for a strong, unconditional advantage for nonviolence. They stress that this is not evidence that nonviolence fails. Chenoweth's defenders can note that she already presents her figures as tendencies. For now you can say something narrower than the slogans: nonviolent mass campaigns have often toppled dictators, but how much more often than armed ones, and why, is an open question.

title: Networked Protest and What Movements Achieve
description: Digital mobilisation, its hidden fragility, and how sociologists measure what movements win

concepts.title: Twitter and Tear Gas
concepts.contentHtml:
From the Arab Spring and Spain's indignados to Occupy Wall Street, the protests of 2011 used digital media to mobilise at astonishing speed. W. Lance Bennett and Alexandra Segerberg called this the logic of connective action (2012): instead of formal organisations recruiting members, personalised content shared across digital networks (a hashtag, an image, a slogan) does much of the coordinating. Black Lives Matter is the emblem of this generation. A Pew Research Center analysis counted more than 44 million #BlackLivesMatter tweets from nearly 10 million distinct users between July 2013 and March 2023.1

The sociologist Zeynep Tufekci, who stood in the tear gas of Istanbul's Gezi Park protests in 2013, gave the most influential account of the costs in Twitter and Tear Gas (2017). Compare the 1963 March on Washington. Its chief logistics organiser, Bayard Rustin, ran an operation in which hundreds of people worked directly on organising for two months, and overall preparation took six months. Today a hashtag can summon protesters instead. But the slow work did more than produce a march. It built what Tufekci calls network internalities: the trust, habits of decision-making and delegation that a group gains by solving problems together over time.

Movements that skip this stage, she argues, are fragile in three ways:

  • Tactical freeze: without a culture or structure for collective decisions, they struggle to change course after the first burst.
  • No one to negotiate: leaderlessness protects them from co-optation and decapitation, but leaves no one able to bargain when an opening comes.
  • Weak signals: authorities read protests as signals of underlying capacity. Montgomery's 13-month boycott signalled the ability to sustain a gruelling campaign; a crowd assembled in days signals far less.2

Governments have adapted too, answering digital tools with misinformation, distraction and surveillance. Tufekci does not call networked movements failures. A great march that was once the climax of years of organising may now be a movement's first step rather than its last.

concepts.title: What Counts as Success?
concepts.contentHtml:
Judging a movement is harder than it looks. In The Strategy of Social Protest (1975), William Gamson drew a representative sample of 53 "challenging groups" that emerged in the United States between 1800 and 1945. He asked two questions: did a group gain new advantages for its constituency, and was it accepted by its antagonists? Thirty-one groups (58 percent) gained new advantages or acceptance, and twenty (38 percent) gained both.1

Gamson's findings surprised many readers:

  • Groups that sought to displace existing elites rarely succeeded.
  • Groups offering selective incentives to members did better, as Olson would predict.
  • Groups using unruly tactics, such as strikes and even violence, did better, especially when the target was weak.
  • Groups with bureaucratic, centralised organisation and no factional splits did better.

The study has been criticised as too simple, and later research widened the idea of an outcome. Movements change policy, but also culture, public opinion and the lives of participants, as Freedom Summer did. Gains can also fade. Pew Research Center surveys found that support for Black Lives Matter among US adults peaked at 67 percent in June 2020 and fell to 55 percent by September 2020. In 2025 it stood at 52 percent, and 72 percent of Americans said the increased focus on race after George Floyd's killing had not led to changes that improved Black people's lives.2

Notice the tension. Gamson found unruliness and even violence associated with winning; Chenoweth found nonviolence associated with winning. The samples differ (American challengers seeking advantages versus campaigns to topple regimes), and both findings are correlations. To learn whether protest itself causes change, you need a way to separate the effect of protest from everything that drives it.

concepts.title: Do Protests Cause Change? Natural Experiments
concepts.contentHtml:
Protest and political change go together, but which causes which? Rallies are bigger where people already agree with them, so a correlation between rallies and later votes might only show that protesters live among sympathisers. The Credibility Revolution topic describes the economist's answer: find something that shifts protest size for reasons unrelated to politics. One such thing is the weather.

On Tax Day, 15 April 2009, the new Tea Party movement held coordinated rallies across the United States. Andreas Madestam, Daniel Shoag, Stan Veuger and David Yanagizawa-Drott (2013) used rainfall on that day as an instrumental variable: rain cut attendance, but a wet day is unlikely to change anyone's politics directly. Places with good weather, and so bigger rallies, later had a stronger local movement, more public support for Tea Party positions and more Republican votes in the 2010 midterm elections, and their members of Congress voted more conservatively. Each additional protester appears to have produced well over one additional Republican vote.1 Protests, the authors concluded, do not merely reveal existing opinion; they build movements that change it.

Omar Wasow (2020) applied similar tools to Black-led protests between 1960 and 1972. Nonviolent activism, particularly when met with state or vigilante repression, drove media coverage, congressional speech and public opinion on civil rights, and counties near nonviolent protests saw the Democratic presidential vote share rise by 1.6 to 2.5 percent. Protester-initiated violence pushed coverage and public concern toward "social control". Using rainfall as an instrument, Wasow estimated that violent protests in 1968 caused a shift of 1.5 to 7.9 percent among white voters toward the Republicans, likely enough to tip the election.

These designs have limits. An instrument is only as good as the assumption that it works solely through protest size, and the estimates apply to particular places and periods. Still, they move the question from belief to evidence, and they point the same way: protest can change politics, and the tactics chosen shape which way it moves.
